speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what is the trend for the total average amount of Government spending on foreign students per year over the past 10 years; and (b) what is the current percentage of foreign students receiving any form of state financial aid out of the total student population (both foreign and local) in polytechnics, junior colleges and autonomous universities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because we plan the number of IHL places with Singaporean students in mind.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This ensures that students can cope with the rigour of the curriculum, the IHL continues to be held in high regard, both locally and internationally, and students are valued by employers upon graduation and they can secure jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When all Singaporean students who meet the standards have been admitted, the IHLs then raise the bar by a few notches and then admit a small minority of international students, over and above the local students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of this method, no Singaporean student is ever displaced from an IHL because of an international student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Beyond the heavy Government subsidies available to all Singaporean students, there is also financial aid, in the form of assistance and bursaries, to ensure that fees remain affordable for lower- to middle-income families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unfortunately, immediately after we issued the written reply, I see online reports with a fabricated and inflated number of over $300 million.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The real cost, actually, is well below $130 million per year, because $130 million is the worth of the scholarships to the students, not the cost to the education system as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us say a restaurant gives a $100 voucher to a customer.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The voucher is worth $100 to the customer, but the incremental cost to the restaurant to fulfil the voucher can be much less.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because the cost of rental, utilities, service staff, management and so on, are more or less fixed already, whether the customer turns up with the voucher or not.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Imagine, if tomorrow we send back all our international students on scholarships, how much of our education budget do we save?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think it would be much less than $130 million, because that is the worth of the scholarships to the international students, not the expenditure incurred by the system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Overhead costs, such as the buildings, laboratories, equipment, management, manpower, faculty will still need to be incurred anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, if we send back all our international students, what we will lose, are the opportunities for Singaporean students to build bonds and bridges with students from other countries and expand their network of friends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is an increasingly important aspect of education because we are all working in a globalised, multicultural world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will also lose a catchment of people who can contribute to Singapore, potentially.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, international students in IHLs who are awarded scholarships are required to work in Singapore for at least three years after they graduate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many eventually sink roots, take up Permanent Residency or citizenship and raise their families here.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even if they decide to leave Singapore after fulfilling their obligations, they can be part of our valuable global network of fans and friends, who can speak up for Singapore from time to time and forge collaborations with Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The third point I want to make is that because of the reasons above, every reputable IHL all around the world admits international students and provides them with some form of financial support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The best universities around the world – Oxford, Yale, Ecole Polytechnique, Technical University of Munich and so on – all have a diverse and international student body, far more than our IHLs, in fact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, there are top United States (US) universities like Yale, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Princeton, who have needs-blind admission system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, they do not admit you based on whether you can pay.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So long as you meet their standards, you are admitted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you cannot pay, there will be some form of donations, financial assistance to help you pay.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singaporean students must have entered those schools on that basis before as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of that, Singaporeans studying overseas benefit from subsidised fees or scholarships from overseas universities as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, many European universities offer free or heavily subsidised education to all foreign students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are around 400 Singaporean students currently studying in French and German universities and they benefit from highly subsidised tuition fees there.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we give some and we also take some.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And our IHLs cannot depart from this international practice norm and has to be part of this global education network.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate that response for the $130 million for scholarships.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do appreciate that that is also, likewise, probably going to be a nominal figure for the reasons that the Minister shared.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is relating to comparisons with other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the original Parliamentary Question reply last month and also as the Minister has clarified, there is some element of reciprocity, so Singaporeans students also benefit from aid.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think some of the cases the Minister cited are aid given by universities rather than aid given by governments and states.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the universities that the Minister mentioned have large endowments and they provide funding to international students who need it, including Singaporean students.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, given this point of reciprocity and being part of the network, can I ask if the Ministry tracks or does the Ministry know what is the comparable amount of governmental spending that other developed countries actually provide to foreign students studying in their countries proportionately as a percentage of their education budget?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third and last one is really on how the impact of Singapore is measured.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry actually look at, over time, the impact of the spending on foreign students and what are, for example, economic multipliers from retaining high quality foreigners to work in the workforce vis-a-vis an alternative, such as recruiting foreigners on the open market to come and work here without making that spending on foreign students in the education system?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the tuition grant, just to let Members know, there are scholarships that we give to foreign students who are very talented and we want them to be part of our system and they have an obligation to work here.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the Member has also pointed out, this is a nominal figure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the worth of the scholarships and tuition grants to the foreign students but does not reflect the cost to our education system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second question, the aid given by universities in other countries is from the universities, whereas for us, it is from the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have state universities, they also have private universities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In our case, all our autonomous universities are all Government-run.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, the circumstances are different; ours is a much more public and centralised system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there is no doubt that all systems around the world use their universities to attract talent from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a fight for talent in the whole world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we cannot run away from that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Has there been any study on impact of spending on foreign students?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would very much welcome the academia or our economists, please do a learned study.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we know this has been beneficial to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Do it in the right proportion, do not overdo it, do not under-do it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because, first, our Singapore students benefit from interacting and making friends with foreign students, building bridges, building bonds and friendships with them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do know, many of us, many of the colleagues we work with, actually might have come to Singapore to study at a fairly young age, sometimes on scholarships and, over time, they sink roots here, have children here, and their children serve National Service.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We see so many of these cases around us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I recently came across an entrepreneur, a successful one from the People's Republic of China (PRC).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He was a foreigner thinking of doing a startup.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then decided to go into it with a good friend, and the partner, in turn, has another friend, a lady, and both of them were PRCs and had studied in Singapore in secondary school.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After that, the partner and the wife said that, "We studied in Singapore, it is a wonderful place, how about you start your business in Singapore?" Therefore, that was what he did.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given the Member's strong interest in this subject, if I may ask him in return a question: may I know what is the Member's or the Member's party's position with regard to international students in our schools and our universities?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Do you advocate a zero international student policy?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I can only speak on my personal view on this and my view would be that a certain amount of spending is certainly justified and that spending has to be calibrated based on the benefits that we receive back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That was the point of my question, to understand what that spending is.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If I recall correctly, there was one incident when the Speaker talked about a quote from former Vice President, Joe Biden, who said that, our spending is a reflection of our priorities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, what we say about our policy goals and objectives is one thing, but our spending really concretely reflects that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To me, it seems on the high side.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I do keep an open mind because I think if the Government can provide reasons that this practice generates, for example, economic multipliers, that we attract foreigners to stay here who would not otherwise come.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But coming down to the exact number, he feels it is on the high side.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if he is the Minister for Education one day, he will send back more international students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there could be other students out there who might be more than willing to come, who can afford to be net-fee payers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is, in fact, something that a lot of universities in the United Kingdom (UK), the US and Australia depend on, that is, a large volume of foreign students who are net-fee payers and who, in fact, subsidise the local students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is the situation in some other countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, although they come and attend our universities, they receive no tuition grant nor scholarship.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, the process is that if you apply to enter the university, you must meet the standard, which is a higher one than locals and, after you are accepted, you can then apply for a tuition grant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And some students choose not to apply for a tuition grant and they do become net-fee payers, and I think this is something we ought to discuss with the universities.
